newsitem.title: USA: Doctors urge Supreme Court to ban assisted-suicide.
newsitem.headline: Doctors urge Supreme Court to ban assisted-suicide.

text.p: Leading U.S. doctors' organisations and more than 30 other health care groups on Tuesday urged the Supreme Court to uphold state bans on physician-assisted suicide.

The American Medical Association (AMA) and other health care groups, including the American Nurses Association and the American Psychiatric Association, said they were filing a friend-of-the-court petition, or amici curiae, in the Supreme Court on Tuesday.

"The real issue for us is that if they want suicide, don't ask physicians to be the participants. We don't think it is ethical -- We are about healing patients," Dr. Tom Reardon, vice chairman of the AMA board of trustees, said in a telephone interview.

Entering a divisive social debate that approaches the contoversy over abortion and capital punishment in emotional intensity, the Supreme Court agreed to decide in its 1996-97 term whether states may ban doctor-assisted suicide.
Advocates say mentally competent, terminally ill patients should be able to seek help from their doctors when they believe the time has come to end their suffering.
Opponents, like the AMA, believe doctors should not be in the business of ending lives and that when a patient's pain and depression are treated, the desire for death often fades.

"If we treat their depression, if we treat their pain, if we are adequately taking care of our patients needs they won't feel the need to ask for suicide," said Reardon, chairman of the AMA task force on assisted suicide, palliation and end-of-life issues.

More than 30 states have made assisted suicide a crime. The Supreme Court is reviewing laws from New York and Washington state, where such bans have been struck down by lower courts as unconstitutional.
The cases before the Supreme Court did not involve retired pathologist Dr. Jack Kevorkian, the best known U.S. advocate of assisted suicide. He has assisted in more than 40 cases.

The Supreme Court last addressed a related issue in 1990, ruling that a person has a constitutional right to refuse unwanted medical treatment in a case involving a comatose woman whose parents wanted to end artifical life support.

But the health care groups that filed the friend-of-the- court brief said there was a difference between refusing treatment, as in that 1990 case, and actively bringing about death in the pending cases.

"Health care professionals are committed to their ethical and legal obligations to honour patient requests to withhold or withdraw unwanted life-prolonging treatment and to provide patients with all medications necessary to alleviate physical pain," said a draft of the doctors' brief.

More than 30 groups signed the brief, including organisations that do not always see eye-to-eye on health policy. "We disagree on some things but we certainly are the ones who are closest to taking care of patients and see no rationale for assisted suicide," Reardon said. "Fundamentally, we think it is unethical."

Australia's Northern Territory legalised assisted suicide earlier this year, upholding the world's first voluntary euthanasia law. It allows terminally ill people to die by lethal injection or pills and went into force on July 1.
